title: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
summary: What Shor and Grover break, lattices and LWE from zero, how ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA work and fail, hybrids, inventory and agility, and the NIST IR 8547 deadlines.
outcomes: Explain what Shor's and Grover's algorithms break, and why RSA and ECC must go while AES-128 stays
Use Mosca's inequality and harvest-now-decrypt-later to decide what to migrate first
Explain lattices, LWE and Module-LWE, and encrypt and decrypt a bit with a toy LWE scheme by hand
Describe how ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA work, their sizes, and pitfalls such as KyberSlash and state reuse
Use ML-KEM and ML-DSA correctly with Go and OpenSSL, including input checks, key derivation and contexts

lessons.title: What a quantum computer breaks, and what it only dents

blocks.md:
Every public-key tool from crypto-building-blocks and tls-pki rests on one of two math problems: **factoring** a large number (RSA) or finding a **discrete logarithm** (finite-field Diffie-Hellman, and its elliptic-curve forms X25519, ECDH, ECDSA and Ed25519). Ordinary computers cannot solve either at real key sizes.

A **quantum computer** computes with *qubits* (quantum bits), which can hold a superposition of 0 and 1, and steers a computation with interference so that wrong answers cancel and right ones reinforce. It is not a faster general-purpose computer: Bas Westerbaan, a cryptographer at Cloudflare, [compares quantum computers to graphics cards](https://blog.cloudflare.com/pq-2024/), specialised devices that are much worse than regular computers at most tasks. Two specific quantum algorithms matter for security.

- **Shor's algorithm** (lesson 2) factors numbers and computes discrete logarithms in a number of steps that grows only polynomially with the key size. RSA, Diffie-Hellman and every elliptic-curve scheme fall to it completely, and because the work grows so slowly, bigger keys are not a fix.
- **Grover's algorithm** (lesson 3) speeds up brute-force search by a square root. It dents symmetric ciphers, hashes and MACs, and NIST concludes that AES with keys of 128 bits or more and SHA-256 do not need replacing.

NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) calls a machine able to run Shor against real key sizes a **CRQC**, a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer; none exists today. The day one arrives is widely called **Q-day**, a term Cloudflare's reports use throughout. **Post-quantum cryptography** (PQC) means ordinary algorithms, running on today's computers, built on math problems for which no fast quantum algorithm is known.

blocks.title: Which primitives fall to which quantum algorithm

scenes.caption: The tools you already use: public-key schemes on top, symmetric primitives at the bottom.
Shor's algorithm solves factoring and discrete logarithms, so every public-key scheme on the top row is broken outright, at any key size.
Grover's algorithm only speeds up search by a square root. NIST rates AES-128 and up, SHA-256 and HMAC as still adequate (lesson 3).
The migration in one picture: replace key exchange with ML-KEM and signatures with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA (lattice and hash-based signature standards, lessons 10 and 11); keep the symmetric layer.

blocks.md: **When must you start? Mosca's inequality.** NIST IR 8547 (its October 2026 transition report) restates what it calls Mosca's theorem, after Michele Mosca, a quantum computing researcher at the University of Waterloo. Let **X** be how many years your data must stay secret, **Y** how many years your migration will take, and **Z** how many years until a CRQC exists. If X + Y is greater than Z, data you protect during the migration will still be worth reading when it becomes readable, so you are already late.

blocks.caption: X: years the data must stay secret. Y: years the migration takes. Z: years until a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer.

blocks.title: Mosca's inequality on a timeline (years from today)

scenes.caption: Y = 6 years of migration, then data encrypted at the end must stay secret for X = 10 more. If a CRQC arrives at Z = 20, secrecy ends at 16: safe.
Same plan, but Z = 12. From year 12 to 16 the recorded data is readable while it still matters: X + Y = 16 is greater than Z = 12.
You cannot change Z or (usually) X. You can shrink Y: switching key exchange to a hybrid that libraries already ship takes 1 year here, and 1 + 10 is less than 12.

blocks.md: Two clocks. **Confidentiality** has the harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) problem from tls-pki: traffic recorded today can be decrypted after Q-day, so **key establishment migrates first**. **Signatures** do not: IR 8547 notes they are not vulnerable to HNDL, because a forged signature is useful only while the old key is still trusted. Signatures are still urgent, because certificates, firmware and devices take longest to change.

One signature case cannot wait: devices whose verification code cannot be updated after manufacture. IR 8547 says that if such a device may still be in use once a CRQC exists, it should be designed now to require quantum-resistant signatures on its firmware. A smart meter or car control unit shipped in 2027 with only an ECDSA public key burned in has no safe way to accept updates in 2040.

blocks.question: Which of these must be replaced because of Shor's algorithm?
options: AES-256-GCM encrypting a database
SHA-256 in a software bill of materials
ECDSA P-256 signatures on your TLS certificates
HMAC-SHA256 on API requests
blocks.explain: ECDSA rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, which Shor solves. The other three are symmetric primitives that Grover only dents, and NIST rates them as still adequate.

blocks.question: Patient records must stay confidential for 25 years. Your migration will take 5 years, and estimates for a CRQC range from 10 to 20 years. What does Mosca's inequality tell you?
options: Even at the late estimate, 25 + 5 = 30 exceeds 20, so records sent with classical key exchange today are already at risk from recorded traffic
Nothing yet: wait until the estimates narrow
Only signatures on the records need to change
Upgrade AES-128 to AES-256 first
blocks.explain: X + Y = 30 is greater than every plausible Z, so harvest-now-decrypt-later already applies. Key establishment protecting these records should move to ML-KEM (in practice a hybrid) first; AES-128 is not the weak point.

lessons.title: Shor's algorithm in outline: factoring is period finding

blocks.md: Peter Shor, then at AT&T Research, presented the algorithm at FOCS (the Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science) in November 1994; the expanded paper is [on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027). It gives quantum algorithms for factoring and for discrete logarithms whose number of steps is polynomial in the number of digits. You do not need quantum mechanics to see why it breaks RSA: the quantum computer solves one narrow subproblem, and old number theory does the rest.

**The reduction (classical).** To factor $N$, pick a random $a$ with $1 < a < N$ that shares no factor with $N$. The sequence $a^0, a^1, a^2, \dots \bmod N$ eventually repeats. Its **period** (Shor's paper calls it the *order* of $a$) is the smallest $r > 0$ with $a^r \equiv 1 \pmod N$. Then $(a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1) = a^r - 1$ is a multiple of $N$. Unless $r$ is odd or $a^{r/2} \equiv -1 \pmod N$, each bracket shares a proper factor with $N$, which the greatest common divisor (gcd, computed fast by Euclid's algorithm) pulls out. Shor's paper notes this reduction is older, from the computer scientist Gary L. Miller in 1976.

blocks.caption: Works when r is even and a to the power r/2 is not congruent to -1 mod N. For a random a this succeeds with good probability; otherwise pick another a.

blocks.title: Period finding by hand: a = 7, N = 15

scenes.caption: We need the period of f(x) = 7^x mod 15. The index above each cell is x.
Compute: 7^0 = 1, 7^1 = 7, 7^2 = 49 = 4 (mod 15), then multiply the last value by 7: 7^3 = 4 x 7 = 28 = 13 (mod 15).
7^4 = 13 x 7 = 91 = 1 (mod 15): the sequence starts over. The period is r = 4.

blocks.md:
**Why a quantum computer is needed.** For a 2048-bit $N$ the period can be astronomically long, so listing the sequence is hopeless, and no known classical method finds $r$ efficiently. Shor's quantum step evaluates $a^x \bmod N$ on a superposition of many values of $x$, then applies a **quantum Fourier transform** (the quantum analogue of the transform that finds frequencies in a signal). The periodic pattern makes amplitudes interfere, so a measurement yields information about $r$ with good probability, and a little classical post-processing finishes the job.

The paper solves discrete logarithms with the same period-finding machinery, applied to a function of two exponents. That is why Diffie-Hellman, X25519, ECDSA and Ed25519 fall along with RSA.

blocks.prompt: You double an RSA modulus from 2048 to 4096 bits. Does that put it out of reach of Shor's algorithm?
blocks.reveal: No. Shor's step count grows polynomially with the number of digits, so a machine that factors 2048-bit numbers needs only polynomially more resources for 4096 bits. Bigger keys buy margin against classical attacks, not against a CRQC. That is why NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA and (EC)DH at every approved strength after 2030 instead of asking for longer keys; the fix is a different hard problem.

blocks.md: **How big a machine?** Physical qubits are noisy, so a usable *logical* qubit is built from many physical ones with error correction, which is why estimates count physical qubits. A 2019 estimate by Craig Gidney, a quantum computing researcher at Google, and Martin Ekerå of KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm said RSA-2048 could be factored in about eight hours with 20 million noisy qubits. In 2025 Gidney [lowered that](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917) to less than a week with fewer than one million, under the same assumptions: a 0.1% gate error rate, a 1 microsecond error-correction cycle and a 10 microsecond control reaction time. Cloudflare's [2025 review](https://blog.cloudflare.com/pq-2025/) observed that the date of Q-day matters less than the deadlines regulators have set (lesson 15).

blocks.title: Published resource estimates for factoring RSA-2048

scenes.caption: Physical noisy qubits needed, in millions: 20 in 2019; fewer than 1 in 2025 (an upper bound). Better algorithms cut the hardware needed by more than 20 times.
The trade: runtime in hours rises from about 8 to under 168 (one week, an upper bound). Fewer qubits, longer run: still under a week per key.

blocks.md: Misconception: "a quantum computer tries every key at once." If that were true, Grover's algorithm would be useless next to brute force. Shor works because factoring hides a **periodic structure** that interference can expose. For search with no structure, no quantum algorithm beats Grover's square-root speedup: earlier work showed this up to a constant factor, and Christof Zalka, in a 1997 paper, [proved](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9711070) Grover's algorithm exactly optimal.

blocks.question: For N = 21 and a = 2, the powers 2^x mod 21 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 11, 1, ... What does the reduction give?
options: r = 3, and the factors appear directly as 3 and 7
r = 6 is even, so the method fails
r = 5, so another a must be tried
blocks.explain: The value 1 recurs at x = 6, so r = 6. Then 2^3 = 8, which is not -1 mod 21 (that would be 20). gcd(8 - 1, 21) = 7 and gcd(8 + 1, 21) = 3, and 21 = 3 x 7. An even r is what the method needs, not a failure.

blocks.question: X25519 key exchange involves no factoring at all. Why does Shor's algorithm still break it?
options: It doesn't: only RSA is affected
Shor's paper also solves discrete logarithms with the same period-finding idea, and X25519 rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm
X25519 secretly uses RSA for authentication
Grover's algorithm breaks 128-bit curves
blocks.explain: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for both factoring and discrete logarithms. Recovering an X25519 private scalar from a recorded public key is a discrete-log problem, which is exactly what harvest-now-decrypt-later relies on.

lessons.title: Grover's algorithm, and why AES-128 is still fine

blocks.md: Lov Grover, then at Bell Labs, showed in 1996 that a quantum computer can find one marked item among $N$ unstructured possibilities in about $\sqrt{N}$ steps, where a classical search must look at $N/2$ of them to succeed half the time ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043)). Zalka proved this optimal: about $\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}$ queries for near-certain success, and no quantum search does better. Key search is unstructured search, so for a $k$-bit key ($N = 2^k$), Grover needs on the order of $2^{k/2}$ steps.

The naive reading is "AES-128 now has 64-bit security, so double every key". Two facts undo it.

1. **The steps are sequential.** Each Grover iteration needs the previous one. Zalka showed the only way to parallelise is to split the key space between independent machines: with $P$ machines each searching $N/P$ keys in $\sqrt{N/P}$ steps, total work grows to $P\sqrt{N/P} = \sqrt{NP}$. Running faster costs more in total.
2. **Each step is expensive.** One iteration evaluates AES inside an error-corrected quantum circuit. NIST's 2016 [call for proposals](https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/Post-Quantum-Cryptography/documents/call-for-proposals-final-dec-2016.pdf) said a quantum gate could cost billions or trillions of times as much as a classical gate.

NIST made this precise with **MAXDEPTH**, a cap on how many quantum gates one computation can perform in series. Its suggested range ran from $2^{40}$ (roughly what envisioned quantum computers could do serially in a year) through $2^{64}$ (what classical computers do serially in a decade) to at most $2^{96}$ (atomic-scale qubits running for a millennium). Under that cap, key search on AES-128 costs about $2^{170}/\text{MAXDEPTH}$ quantum gates, against $2^{143}$ classical gates.

blocks.code:
# NIST's 2016 estimates for breaking AES by key search, as log2(gates).
# Quantum (Grover) cost is 2^c / MAXDEPTH: a cap on how long one quantum
# computation can run serially forces the search to be split up.
QUANTUM_C = {"AES-128": 170, "AES-192": 233, "AES-256": 298}
CLASSICAL = {"AES-128": 143, "AES-192": 207, "AES-256": 272}

for depth in (40, 64, 96):               # log2(MAXDEPTH) values NIST discussed
    row = [f"{a}: 2^{QUANTUM_C[a] - depth} quantum gates" for a in QUANTUM_C]
    print(f"MAXDEPTH 2^{depth}: " + ", ".join(row))
print("classical:", ", ".join(f"{a}: 2^{c}" for a, c in CLASSICAL.items()))

# Output:
# MAXDEPTH 2^40: AES-128: 2^130 quantum gates, AES-192: 2^193 quantum gates, AES-256: 2^258 quantum gates
# MAXDEPTH 2^64: AES-128: 2^106 quantum gates, AES-192: 2^169 quantum gates, AES-256: 2^234 quantum gates
# MAXDEPTH 2^96: AES-128: 2^74 quantum gates, AES-192: 2^137 quantum gates, AES-256: 2^202 quantum gates
# classical: AES-128: 2^143, AES-192: 2^207, AES-256: 2^272
blocks.caption: NIST's 2016 estimates turned into numbers (Python 3, real output). Even at the most generous depth limit, AES-128 still needs about 2^74 error-corrected quantum gates, each far costlier than a classical gate. NIST adds that the formula may understate AES's quantum security at very large depths.

blocks.title: Cost to break AES by key search under a depth limit

scenes.caption: AES-128: the quantum line falls as the allowed depth grows, because a longer serial run needs fewer parallel machines. At depth 2^64 it is 2^106 gates.

AES-256 sits more than 120 doublings higher everywhere. Both stay far beyond reach, which is why NIST uses AES-128 as the yardstick for security category 1 (defined below) rather than calling it broken.

blocks.md: NIST's verdict in IR 8547: symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security meet **security category 1** (the lowest of NIST's five post-quantum levels, listed next), and NIST does not expect to transition away from them. Only the few 112-bit ones are disallowed in 2030. Spend the migration budget on RSA and elliptic curves, not on re-keying AES-128.

**Security categories.** Because quantum costs are uncertain, NIST rates every post-quantum parameter set against a symmetric reference instead of in bits:

1. at least as hard as key search on AES-128
2. as a collision on SHA-256
3. as key search on AES-192
4. as a collision on a 384-bit hash (SHA3-384 in IR 8547)
5. as key search on AES-256

ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 are categories 1, 3 and 5. ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 are 2, 3 and 5. NIST recommends **ML-KEM-768** as the default parameter set.

Some policies still require AES-256 everywhere. Cloudflare's 2025 review points out that doubling a symmetric key typically costs far less than double, so that is a cheap safety margin, but it is a policy choice, not something Grover forces. Do not let it delay the public-key work.

blocks.question: A colleague says Grover cuts AES-128 to 64-bit security, so it must be replaced before RSA. What is the best reply?
options: Grover's 2^64 steps run in series, parallelise badly and each is a costly quantum circuit; NIST rates AES-128 category 1, while Shor breaks RSA outright, so fix RSA key exchange first
Agreed: 64-bit keys are brute-forceable today
Grover does not apply to block ciphers at all
Switch to AES-192, which Grover cannot attack
blocks.explain: Grover gives at most a square-root speedup that cannot be parallelised efficiently (Zalka), and NIST's MAXDEPTH analysis keeps AES-128 far out of reach. Shor breaks RSA and ECC entirely, and recorded traffic is exposed now.

blocks.question: Using NIST's 2016 estimate of 2^170 / MAXDEPTH quantum gates, what does key search on AES-128 cost if MAXDEPTH is 2^64?
options: 2^64 gates
2^143 gates
2^106 gates
2^170 gates
blocks.explain: 170 - 64 = 106. A depth cap of 2^64 forces the search to be split across many machines, and the total rises well above the naive 2^64.

lessons.title: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks

blocks.md:
If not factoring or discrete logarithms, then what? Post-quantum schemes rest on problems with no known fast quantum algorithm. The main families:

- **Lattice-based**: noisy linear algebra on high-dimensional grids (lessons 5 to 10). ML-KEM and ML-DSA; Falcon, which NIST is turning into a further signature standard, FN-DSA.
- **Hash-based**: signatures that rely only on a hash function (lesson 11). SLH-DSA, LMS, XMSS.
- **Code-based**: decoding error-correcting codes. HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), chosen in March 2025 as a backup KEM; Classic McEliece also reached the fourth round.
- **Multivariate**: solving systems of quadratic equations in many variables. Rainbow (broken, below); UOV (Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar), MAYO and SNOVA are in NIST's additional signature round.
- **Isogeny-based**: secret maps (isogenies) between elliptic curves. SIKE (Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation; broken, below).

**The competition.** NIST issued its call for proposals in 2016 and assessed 82 algorithms from 25 countries. In July 2022 its third-round report ([NIST IR 8413](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8413/upd1/final)) selected CRYSTALS-Kyber for key establishment and CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON and SPHINCS+ for signatures, recommending Dilithium as the primary signature, and sent four KEMs (BIKE, Bit Flipping Key Encapsulation; Classic McEliece; HQC; SIKE) to a fourth round. CRYSTALS stands for Cryptographic Suite for Algebraic Lattices, the project behind Kyber and Dilithium.

On 13 August 2024 NIST published **FIPS 203** (ML-KEM, from Kyber), **FIPS 204** (ML-DSA, from Dilithium) and **FIPS 205** (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+). FIPS are Federal Information Processing Standards, the US government's computer security standards.

blocks.title: The candidates, the breaks and the standards

scenes.caption: A few of the candidates by family (simplified: there were 82 submissions). Each family bets on a different hard problem.
February 2022: Ward Beullens recovers Rainbow keys for its level-1 parameters in about 53 hours on a laptop. Rainbow was one of three signature finalists.
July 2022: NIST selects Kyber, Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+, and sends BIKE (not shown), Classic McEliece, HQC and SIKE to a fourth round.
30 July 2022: Castryck and Decru post a classical key-recovery attack on SIDH, the protocol inside SIKE. Weeks after advancing, SIKE is dead.
2024 to 2026: three FIPS published, HQC picked as the backup KEM (March 2025), and a standard derived from Falcon in development.

blocks.md:
**Case: SIKE broken on a laptop (2022).** SIKE was the key-encapsulation form of SIDH (Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman). Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru, researchers at KU Leuven in Belgium, posted [an efficient key recovery attack on SIDH](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/975) on 30 July 2022. It exploits extra information that SIDH public keys reveal (where the secret map sends certain auxiliary points), using a theorem of the mathematician Ernst Kani. The final version of their paper, published at Eurocrypt 2023, breaks SIKEp434, the level-1 parameter set, in about ten minutes on a single core. No quantum computer was involved.

**Case: Rainbow (2022).** The paper ["Breaking Rainbow Takes a Weekend on a Laptop"](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/214), by Ward Beullens of IBM Research Zurich, gave new key-recovery attacks that beat earlier attacks for every submitted parameter set and are practical for the level-1 parameters of the second-round submission: about 53 hours on average on a standard laptop.

What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

Misconception: "an algorithm is quantum-safe until someone builds a quantum computer that breaks it." Both 2022 breaks ran on ordinary computers. Confidence in ML-KEM and ML-DSA comes from years of public cryptanalysis of lattice problems, and NIST still hedged with HQC, which it says is based on different math than ML-KEM.

blocks.question: SIKE was broken in 2022. What did the attack require?
options: A quantum computer with a few thousand qubits
Only an ordinary computer: the final paper reports about ten minutes on one core for SIKEp434
Access to the victim's random number generator
A timing side channel on the decapsulating server
blocks.explain: Castryck and Decru's attack is a classical mathematical key recovery that uses the extra information in SIDH public keys. It needed no special access, which is why it ended SIKE rather than just one implementation.

blocks.question: Why did NIST select HQC in March 2025 when ML-KEM was already standardised?
options: HQC is faster and smaller than ML-KEM
Because HQC is the only KEM approved for hybrids
Because ML-KEM was broken
As a backup based on different math (error-correcting codes), in case a weakness is found in ML-KEM
blocks.explain: NIST's announcement calls HQC a second line of defence and says ML-KEM remains the recommended choice. Cloudflare's 2025 review adds that HQC is larger and slower on every metric, so it is insurance rather than a replacement.

lessons.title: Lattices from zero: points, bases and hard problems

blocks.md: A **lattice** is the set of all integer combinations of some linearly independent vectors; those vectors are a **basis**. With $b_1 = (2,0)$ and $b_2 = (1,2)$ the lattice is every point $a\,b_1 + c\,b_2$ for integers $a$ and $c$: $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(1,2)$, $(3,2)$, $(4,4)$ and so on, a regular grid that need not be square. This is the definition used by Oded Regev, a computer scientist then at Tel Aviv University, in the 2005 paper that introduced LWE (below), with $n$ vectors in $n$ dimensions.

A lattice has many bases. $(4,4)$ and $(5,6)$ generate **the same points** as $(2,0)$ and $(1,2)$: $(4,4) = b_1 + 2b_2$ and $(5,6) = b_1 + 3b_2$, and going back, $b_1 = 3(4,4) - 2(5,6)$ and $b_2 = -(4,4) + (5,6)$. Both pairs span parallelograms of area 4 (their determinant).

The first basis is short and nearly perpendicular: a **good basis**. The second is long and nearly parallel: a **bad basis**. Both describe the lattice perfectly; only one makes questions about it easy to answer.

blocks.title: A two-dimensional lattice, two bases and two hard problems

scenes.caption: The lattice generated by (2,0) and (1,2), drawn as (column, row) with rows counting downward. Every circle is an integer combination of the basis.
Good basis: b1 = (2,0) and b2 = (1,2), short and close to perpendicular. Walking from 0 by whole steps of b1 and b2 reaches every point.
Bad basis: (4,4) and (5,6). Long and nearly parallel, yet it generates exactly the same points. A public key can look like this.
SVP (shortest vector problem): find the shortest non-zero lattice point. Here (2,0), length 2. Easy to see in 2D; hard in hundreds of dimensions.
CVP (closest vector problem): given a target t = (3,5) that is not a lattice point, find the nearest lattice point: (3,6), distance 1.

blocks.md: In two dimensions you see the answers. Real schemes work in hundreds of dimensions: an ML-KEM-768 secret has $3 \times 256 = 768$ coefficients. There, given only a bad basis, the best known algorithms for the approximate versions of SVP and CVP that cryptography relies on, classical or quantum, take time exponential in the dimension. That is the bet behind lattice cryptography.

**From grids to equations: LWE.** Schemes do not hand you a basis; they hand you noisy equations, which are lattice problems in disguise. **LWE** (learning with errors), introduced by Regev in 2005, works like this: a secret vector $s$ of numbers mod $q$, many random vectors $a_i$, and values $b_i$ that are the dot product $\langle a_i, s\rangle$ plus a **small error** $e_i$. Regev describes it as a natural extension of the older "learning from parity with error" problem from bits to larger moduli.

blocks.tex: b_i = \langle a_i, s \rangle + e_i \bmod q, \qquad e_i \text{ small (for example } -1, 0, 1)
blocks.caption: Without the errors e_i this is an ordinary linear system. With them, recovering s is believed hard even for quantum computers.

blocks.prompt: An attacker sees 1,000 such equations in 500 unknowns mod q. How hard is recovering s with no errors, and with errors of size 1?
blocks.reveal: With **no errors**, it is school algebra: Gaussian elimination solves the system in polynomial time, as Regev's paper notes. With **small errors**, elimination combines many equations, and their errors add up until the result is noise. Regev showed that solving LWE efficiently would give a quantum algorithm for worst-case lattice problems such as GapSVP (a decision version of SVP). That reduction from the hardest lattice instances is the main reason cryptographers trust LWE.

blocks.md: The lattice trapdoor in one sentence: the **public key** is a pile of noisy equations, the **private key** is the secret that turns the noise back into something small, and encryption hides a message under more noise that only the key holder can strip away (next lesson, by hand).

blocks.question: The bases {(2,0), (1,2)} and {(4,4), (5,6)} are compared. Which statement is true?
options: They generate exactly the same lattice; the first is a good basis and the second a bad one
They generate different lattices because the vectors differ
Only the second basis can be used for cryptography
The bad basis has a larger determinant
blocks.explain: Each pair is an integer combination of the other, so the lattices are identical, and both have determinant 4. The difference is how useful each basis is for solving SVP or CVP.

blocks.question: Why does adding small errors to random linear equations make the secret hard to find?
options: Errors make the equations inconsistent, so no secret exists
Errors make the numbers too large to store
Elimination has to combine many equations, and the combined errors grow until the answer is hidden; no efficient method is known
The errors are encrypted with AES
blocks.explain: A secret still satisfies every equation up to small errors, so it exists. What breaks is the efficient algorithm: combining equations amplifies the noise, and the best known attacks are lattice algorithms that take exponential time in the dimension.

lessons.title: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand

blocks.md:
Regev's 2005 cryptosystem turns LWE into public-key encryption, and the paper sums it up in one sentence: publish a list of noisy equations as the public key; to encrypt, add up some of the equations and shift the right-hand side depending on the message.

1. **Key generation.** Secret $s$ (here 3 numbers mod $q = 41$). Public key: $m = 6$ rows $(a_i, b_i)$ with $b_i = \langle a_i, s \rangle + e_i$, each error in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.
2. **Encrypt a bit $\mu$.** Pick a random subset of rows ($r_i \in \{0,1\}$). Send $u = \sum r_i a_i$ and $v = \sum r_i b_i + \mu \lfloor q/2 \rfloor$, all mod $q$.
3. **Decrypt.** Compute $d = v - \langle u, s\rangle$. The $s$ parts cancel, leaving only the summed noise, plus 20 if the bit was 1. Near 0 means 0; near 20 means 1.

blocks.tex: d = v - \langle u, s\rangle \equiv \sum_i r_i e_i + \mu \left\lfloor \tfrac{q}{2} \right\rfloor \pmod q
blocks.caption: Correct whenever the summed noise stays below q/4 in size. Here at most 6 rows each add at most 1, so the noise is at most 6, below 41/4.

blocks.title: The public key (A | b) and the rows each encryption sums

scenes.caption: Secret s = (2, 33, 7). Column b here shows the noise-free values a.s mod 41. Publishing these would let anyone solve for s by elimination.
Add noise e = (-1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1) to the last column: b = (19, 30, 23, 13, 10, 25). This (A | b) is the public key.
Encrypt bit 0: the subset is rows 1, 2, 5. u = (24, 21, 34) and v = 30 + 23 + 25 = 78 = 37 (mod 41). Decrypt: d = 1, the summed noise 1 + 1 - 1. Near 0: bit 0.
Encrypt bit 1: rows 2, 3, 4, 5, so u = (3, 14, 8) and v = 71 + 20 = 91 = 9 (mod 41). Decrypt: d = 18 = 20 - 2 (noise 1 - 1 - 1 - 1). Near 20: bit 1.

blocks.code:
# TOY LWE encryption of one bit (Regev 2005 style). Insecure by design.
import random
random.seed(19)
q, n, m = 41, 3, 6                                  # modulus, secret size, rows
s = [random.randrange(q) for _ in range(n)]         # private key
A = [[random.randrange(q) for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(m)]
e = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) for _ in range(m)]   # small noise
b = [(sum(a*x for a, x in zip(row, s)) + ei) % q for row, ei in zip(A, e)]
print("s =", s, " e =", e)                          # public key is (A, b)

def encrypt(bit):
    r = [random.choice([0, 1]) for _ in range(m)]   # random subset of rows
    u = [sum(ri*A[i][j] for i, ri in enumerate(r)) % q for j in range(n)]
    v = (sum(ri*bi for ri, bi in zip(r, b)) + bit*(q//2)) % q
    return r, u, v

def decrypt(u, v):
    d = (v - sum(uj*sj for uj, sj in zip(u, s))) % q  # = noise + bit*20
    return d, int(q//4 < d < 3*q//4)                  # near 20 means 1

for bit in (0, 1):
    r, u, v = encrypt(bit)
    d, out = decrypt(u, v)
    print(f"bit {bit}: r={r} u={u} v={v} v-u.s={d} decrypts to {out}")

# Output:
# s = [2, 33, 7]  e = [-1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1]
# bit 0: r=[0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1] u=[24, 21, 34] v=37 v-u.s=1 decrypts to 0
# bit 1: r=[0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] u=[3, 14, 8] v=9 v-u.s=18 decrypts to 1
blocks.caption: A runnable toy in Python 3 (real output). The numbers match the matrix above. It is a classroom model of the math, not a scheme to use.

blocks.md: **Why the noise budget matters.** Every row added to $u$ and $v$ adds its error. Decryption is right only while the total stays inside the quarter of the circle around 0 or around $q/2$. Add too many rows, or allow larger errors, and some ciphertexts decrypt to the wrong bit: a **decryption failure**. Real schemes tune $q$, the dimension and the error distribution so failures are astronomically rare; FIPS 203 gives decapsulation failure rates of $2^{-138.8}$, $2^{-164.8}$ and $2^{-174.8}$ for ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024.

**Why the toy is insecure.** Three reasons, each fixed in ML-KEM:

- **Tiny dimension.** With 3 unknowns mod 41 there are only $41^3 = 68{,}921$ possible secrets, so brute force works. ML-KEM uses 512 to 1024 coefficients.
- **One bit per big ciphertext.** ML-KEM packs 256 bits into one ciphertext using polynomials (next lesson).
- **Only passive security.** This scheme is IND-CPA (indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack, meaning safe against eavesdroppers). An active attacker who sends modified ciphertexts to a key holder and watches the results can learn the key: RFC 9954 warns that some IND-CPA lattice KEMs leak the private key after a few thousand such queries. ML-KEM adds a transform against exactly this.

This toy exists to make the math visible. Never write your own lattice cryptography for real use: use ML-KEM from a maintained library (lesson 8), whose implementers also handle constant-time code, input checks and randomness.

blocks.question: In the toy (q = 41), decrypting an encryption of bit 1 gives d = 18. Why is that read as 1?
options: Because 18 is even
Because the secret s was used
Because d is never 0 for bit 1
Because 18 lies between 10 and 30, the band around q/2 = 20; the extra -2 is summed noise
blocks.explain: Decryption checks which of 0 or 20 the value is closer to (the band 10 < d < 30 means 1). The 2 missing from 20 is the sum of the errors of the chosen rows.

blocks.question: You change the toy to use 60 rows instead of 6, with the same errors in {-1, 0, 1} and q = 41. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: more rows always add security
Summed noise can now exceed q/4, so some ciphertexts decrypt to the wrong bit
Encryption becomes impossible
The secret becomes public
blocks.explain: With 60 rows, the worst-case noise is 60, far above 41/4. Real parameter sets balance noise against modulus so failures are negligible, which is what FIPS 203's failure rates quantify.

lessons.title: Inside ML-KEM: modules, compression and the FO transform

blocks.md:
ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, FIPS 203) is the toy of lesson 6 made compact and safe against active attackers. Four changes:

1. **Polynomials instead of numbers.** Each "number" becomes a polynomial with 256 coefficients mod $q = 3329$, multiplied in the ring $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^{256}+1)$, where $X^{256}$ wraps around to $-1$. One product mixes all 256 coefficients, so keys shrink. The **NTT** (number-theoretic transform) is a change of representation that makes these products fast.
2. **Modules.** The secret is a vector of $k$ such polynomials ($k$ = 2, 3, 4 for ML-KEM-512, -768, -1024) and the matrix $A$ is $k \times k$. Security rests on **Module-LWE (MLWE)**: LWE over this module, hence "module-lattice".
3. **A seeded matrix.** $A$ is never sent: a 32-byte seed $\rho$ in the public key regenerates it.
4. **Compression.** Ciphertext coefficients are rounded to $d_u$ (10 or 11) and $d_v$ (4 or 5) bits, trading a little extra noise for size.

blocks.caption: K-PKE, the inner encryption scheme: the same shape as lesson 6, with y choosing the combination and one message bit in each of the 256 coefficients, so m is 32 bytes.

blocks.md:
**From encryption to a KEM: the FO transform.** K-PKE on its own is only safe against eavesdroppers, and FIPS 203 forbids using it alone. ML-KEM wraps it in the **Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform**, named after Eiichiro Fujisaki and Tatsuaki Okamoto, NTT cryptographers who proposed it in 1999:

- **Encaps**: choose 32 random bytes $m$; derive $(K, r) = G(m \,\|\, H(ek))$ with SHA-3 based hashes; encrypt $m$ with K-PKE using $r$ as all of its randomness. Output the key $K$ and ciphertext $c$.
- **Decaps**: decrypt to $m'$, recompute $(K', r')$, **re-encrypt** $m'$ with $r'$ and compare with $c$. If equal, output $K'$. If not, output $J(z \,\|\, c)$, a pseudorandom value from a secret $z$ stored in the decapsulation key. This is **implicit rejection**: a forged ciphertext yields a useless key, never an error message an attacker could learn from.

The result is believed IND-CCA2 secure: indistinguishable even under adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack, the active-attacker model the toy failed.

blocks.title: ML-KEM.Decaps: decrypt, re-encrypt, compare

nodes.label:
re-encrypt m'
with r', gives c'

scenes.caption: An honest ciphertext. Decrypting gives m', hashing m' gives the key candidate K' and the exact randomness r' the sender must have used.
Re-encrypting m' with r' reproduces c bit for bit, so the ciphertext was formed honestly. Output K', the same 32 bytes the sender got.
An attacker flips one bit of c. Decryption may still give a plausible m', but the re-encryption cannot match the altered c.
Implicit rejection: output J(z || c), 32 bytes unrelated to K. The caller sees no error, and FIPS 203 forbids revealing which branch was taken.

blocks.title: ML-KEM sizes on the wire, with X25519 for scale (bytes)

scenes.caption: Encapsulation key (the public key): 800, 1184, 1568 bytes, against 32 for an X25519 public key.
Ciphertext: 768, 1088, 1568 bytes, against X25519's 32-byte reply. Every ML-KEM shared secret is 32 bytes.

blocks.md: **Parameter sets (FIPS 203, Table 2).** All use $n = 256$ and $q = 3329$. ML-KEM-512: $k = 2$, $\eta_1 = 3$, $\eta_2 = 2$, $d_u = 10$, $d_v = 4$. ML-KEM-768: $k = 3$, $\eta_1 = \eta_2 = 2$, $d_u = 10$, $d_v = 4$. ML-KEM-1024: $k = 4$, $\eta_1 = \eta_2 = 2$, $d_u = 11$, $d_v = 5$. The $\eta$ values set the width of the small-noise distribution (a centred binomial). Bigger $k$ means more dimensions, more security and bigger keys.

Name the keys the way FIPS 203 does: **encapsulation key** (ek, public) and **decapsulation key** (dk, secret). ML-KEM.KeyGen starts from two random 32-byte seeds $(d, z)$, and Go's crypto/mlkem stores just this 64-byte seed as the private key; OpenSSL's default private-key file holds the seed plus the expanded decapsulation key. The seed regenerates everything, so protect it exactly like the full decapsulation key.

blocks.question: Why does ML-KEM.Decaps re-encrypt the message it just decrypted?
options: To detect ciphertexts that were not produced honestly from some m: only then does c' equal c, and otherwise implicit rejection returns an unrelated key
To double-check the decryption arithmetic
To refresh the decapsulation key
Because K-PKE.Decrypt is randomised
blocks.explain: The FO transform makes the ciphertext a deterministic function of m and ek. Re-encryption checks that, which is what blocks the chosen-ciphertext probing that breaks plain LWE encryption.

blocks.question: A developer wants to use K-PKE directly to encrypt 32-byte messages because it is simpler than the KEM. What does FIPS 203 say?
options: It is approved for short messages
K-PKE shall not be used as a stand-alone scheme; it is only a component of ML-KEM
It is allowed only with ML-KEM-1024
It is approved if the messages are random
blocks.explain: FIPS 203 Section 3.3 states that K-PKE is not approved as a public-key encryption scheme. It is not IND-CCA2 secure; the KEM is.

blocks.md:
FIPS 203 and NIST SP 800-227 (*Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms*, September 2025) turn into a short checklist for anyone writing code against a KEM:

1. **Use a maintained, preferably validated library.** Never K-PKE alone, never your own implementation.
2. **Let the library draw the randomness.** The derandomized `_internal` functions in FIPS 203 are for testing only.
3. **Check inputs.** Encapsulation must run only on an encapsulation key that passed the length and modulus checks; good libraries do this when they parse the key.
4. **Guard the 64-byte seed** like the private key it is.
5. **Derive keys.** The 32-byte shared secret may be used directly as a key, but if you need more keys, derive them with an approved KDF (key derivation function) and a purpose label.
6. **A KEM does not authenticate.** If you encapsulate to someone's long-term key, you must be sure it is theirs (a certificate or signed key), and the exchange needs integrity protection (SP 800-227 requirements RM3 and RM5).
7. **Ephemeral key pairs are used once** and then destroyed (requirement RS6).

blocks.caption: Go 1.24's standard library crypto/mlkem (real output). Go offers ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 and stores the decapsulation key as the 64-byte (d, z) seed. crypto/hkdf derives a purpose-bound key.

blocks.title: Encrypting to a public key with ML-KEM plus an AEAD

scenes.caption: The receiver runs KeyGen, keeps the 64-byte seed secret and publishes ek, ideally inside a certificate or signed record so the sender knows whose key it is.
The sender checks ek (parsing does the modulus check), runs Encaps, derives an AES key with HKDF and encrypts the message with AES-GCM.
One message carries the 1088-byte KEM ciphertext and the AEAD ciphertext. The ML-KEM ciphertext can also go in the AEAD's associated data.
The receiver decapsulates, derives the same key and opens the AEAD. The tag check proves the message and the key both arrived intact.
If a network attacker flips a bit in ct, Decaps still returns 32 bytes (implicit rejection), but the wrong ones: the AEAD tag check fails and the message is rejected.

blocks.caption: The three ways bad input shows up in Go's crypto/mlkem (real output). Only the tampered ciphertext is silent, which is why ML-KEM is always followed by an authenticated step.

blocks.code:
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-KEM-768 -out dk.pem
openssl pkey -in dk.pem -pubout -out ek.pem
openssl pkeyutl -encap -pubin -inkey ek.pem -out ct.bin -secret ss_sender.bin
openssl pkeyutl -decap -inkey dk.pem -in ct.bin -secret ss_receiver.bin
wc -c ct.bin ss_sender.bin
cmp ss_sender.bin ss_receiver.bin && echo "shared secrets match"
openssl pkey -in dk.pem -text -noout | grep -E "seed|Private"

# Output:
#     1088 ct.bin
#       32 ss_sender.bin
#     1120 total
# shared secrets match
# ML-KEM-768 Private-Key:
# seed:
blocks.caption: The same flow with the OpenSSL 4.1 command line (real output). OpenSSL 3.5 added ML-KEM; by default its private-key file holds both the seed and the expanded key, and -text prints the seed first.

blocks.md: Two misconceptions. "**ML-KEM encrypts my message**": no, it transports a fresh random secret; your data is encrypted with an AEAD keyed from that secret. Standards such as HPKE (Hybrid Public Key Encryption, RFC 9180) package this KEM-then-AEAD pattern with the details done right. "**Decapsulate returned no error, so the ciphertext is genuine**": no, implicit rejection means a forged ciphertext also returns 32 bytes.

Defender view. **Prevent**: pin library versions that implement final FIPS 203 (not pre-standard Kyber, which is incompatible), default to ML-KEM-768, and keep decapsulation keys and seeds in a KMS (key management service) or HSM. **Detect**: log algorithm identifiers and key-parse failures; a burst of invalid encapsulation keys or wrong-length ciphertexts is either a bug or probing. **Respond**: rotate static KEM keys after any suspected exposure, as you would any private key.

blocks.question: Your Go service decapsulates an incoming ciphertext and gets no error. What does that tell you?
options: The ciphertext came from the holder of the encapsulation key
The sender has been authenticated
Only that the ciphertext had the right length; a tampered one also returns a 32-byte secret, so integrity comes from the AEAD or protocol that follows
The shared secret has been confirmed by both sides
blocks.explain: ML-KEM uses implicit rejection: invalid ciphertexts give a pseudorandom secret rather than an error. Only a later MAC or AEAD check, or a protocol's key confirmation, shows that both sides hold the same key.

blocks.question: A protocol needs separate keys for each direction from one ML-KEM shared secret. What is the right approach?
options: Derive each key with HKDF (or another approved KDF) using a distinct label such as 'client to server v1'
Split the 32 bytes into two 16-byte keys
Use the 32-byte secret for both directions
Encrypt the secret with itself
blocks.explain: FIPS 203 says further keys shall be derived in an approved way (SP 800-108 or SP 800-56C). Distinct labels give independent keys and bind each to its purpose.

lessons.title: KyberSlash: when one division leaks the key

blocks.md: A correct algorithm can still leak its key through **timing**. At the end of 2023 it emerged that many Kyber libraries, including the official reference code, divided a **secret** number by the public constant $q$. The researchers who documented it (Daniel J. Bernstein, Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Shivam Bhasin, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Tee Kiah Chia, Matthias J. Kannwischer, Franziskus Kiefer, Thales Paiva, Prasanna Ravi and Goutam Tamvada) named the bug [KyberSlash](https://kyberslash.cr.yp.to/): the slash is the division sign.

The division sits in the step you did by hand in lesson 6: decryption asks, for each coefficient $t$, "is this nearer 0 or $q/2$?", computed as $\lfloor (2t + \lfloor q/2 \rfloor)/q \rfloor \bmod 2$. On many CPUs a division instruction takes a different number of cycles depending on its operands, so the decryption time depends on secret values.

- **KyberSlash1** is this division in decryption. **KyberSlash2** is similar divisions in the compression step of encryption, which decapsulation also runs on secret data.
- The authors' [paper](https://kyberslash.cr.yp.to/papers.html) (CHES 2025 best paper) recovered complete Kyber secret keys on a Raspberry Pi 2 and an Arm Cortex-M4: within minutes for KyberSlash2, a few hours for KyberSlash1.
- The reference code was patched on 1 December 2023 (KyberSlash1) and 30 December 2023 (KyberSlash2).

blocks.caption: The vulnerable line and its fix, from the KyberSlash FAQ and the current pq-crystals reference poly.c. Multiplying by 80635 and shifting right by 28 approximates dividing by 3329 closely enough to give the identical bit for every possible t.

blocks.title: Why the time depends on t (simplified model of an AMD Zen 2)

scenes.caption: Six possible secret coefficients t (0 to 3328) reaching the rounding step during decryption.
The numerator 2t + 1664 is what gets divided by 3329.
The result bit: 1 when t is near q/2, 0 when t is near 0 or near q. This is the correct, intended output.
The FAQ reports that on AMD Zen 2 division takes one more cycle once the numerator reaches 8192. The time now depends on t itself, not only on the output bit.
An attacker who controls ciphertexts and times many decapsulations can turn such differences into key bits. The fix removes the division, so every t takes the same time.

blocks.code:
# Check that the patched, division-free line computes exactly the same bit
# as the old division for every coefficient value t in 0..q-1.
q = 3329
old = lambda t: (((t << 1) + q // 2) // q) & 1           # secret / public: variable time on some CPUs
new = lambda t: ((((t << 1) + 1665) * 80635) >> 28) & 1  # multiply and shift only
print("identical for all t:", all(old(t) == new(t) for t in range(q)))
print("bit for t = 0, 832, 833, 1664, 2496, 2497, 3328:",
      [new(t) for t in (0, 832, 833, 1664, 2496, 2497, 3328)])

# Output:
# identical for all t: True
# bit for t = 0, 832, 833, 1664, 2496, 2497, 3328: [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0]
blocks.caption: Checking the fix exhaustively (Python 3, real output). This verifies the arithmetic only; Python itself is not constant-time, so timing must be tested on the compiled C.

blocks.md: Constant time is a property of the **machine code**, not the source. The FAQ notes that on Intel and AMD, gcc -O3 turns this division by a constant into a multiplication while gcc -Os keeps a division instruction; on RISC-V both keep it; on the Raspberry Pi 2 the compiler called a software division routine that branches on its inputs. Some CPUs even multiply in variable time. Test the binary you ship, on the CPUs you ship to.

**Who was exposed.** The FAQ says using each key only once blocks the published demos, though it still says "patch now". TLS key exchange uses fresh ephemeral keys, and Cloudflare noted that KyberSlash did not affect Kyber as used in TLS. The exposed case is a **static decapsulation key** that an attacker can make decapsulate many chosen ciphertexts while timing it: a server's long-term KEM key, a messaging prekey reused for many sessions, an embedded device.

Defender view. **Prevent**: use libraries free of secret divisions (the [KyberSlash libraries page](https://kyberslash.cr.yp.to/libraries.html) lists patch dates) and run variable-time checkers in CI: the authors patched Valgrind (a tool that checks programs as they run) for this and ran it over 1000+ implementations in the SUPERCOP benchmark suite. **Detect**: check your SBOM for affected library versions. **Respond**: upgrade, then rotate static ML-KEM keys that served untrusted clients.

blocks.question: Which deployment was most exposed to KyberSlash?
options: A browser doing hybrid TLS with a fresh key share per connection
A laptop verifying ML-DSA signatures
A server that only encapsulates to clients' keys
An embedded device with one long-term Kyber decapsulation key that decapsulates ciphertexts from anyone on the network
blocks.explain: The attack needs many timed decapsulations under the same secret key. Ephemeral TLS keys block that; a static key reachable by attackers does not.

blocks.question: Why does replacing / by multiply-and-shift fix KyberSlash?
options: Multiplication is faster, so timing differences are too small to measure
It changes the output so attackers cannot predict it
The division instruction's running time depended on its secret operand on many CPUs; the multiply-and-shift sequence computes the same bit without that instruction
It adds random delays
blocks.explain: The fix removes the data-dependent instruction while producing the identical bit for every t. The FAQ still warns that a few CPUs have variable-time multipliers, so the target hardware matters.

lessons.title: ML-DSA: lattice signatures that sometimes start over

blocks.md:
**Schnorr in one paragraph.** FIPS 204 explains ML-DSA through the older Schnorr signature over a discrete-log group with generator $g$, private key $x$ and public key $y = g^x$. The signer **commits** to a random $r$ by computing $g^r$, gets a **challenge** $c$, and sends the **response** $s = r - cx$; a verifier checks $g^s y^c = g^r$. The **Fiat-Shamir** trick (from Amos Fiat and Adi Shamir, 1986) replaces the verifier's random challenge with a hash of the commitment and the message, so the signer can do it alone.

**ML-DSA** (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 204, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) runs the same pattern over module lattices. The public key is essentially $t = A s_1 + s_2$ with small secret vectors $s_1, s_2$: an MLWE instance, as in ML-KEM. FIPS 204 bases security on MLWE and a variant of MSIS (Module Short Integer Solution: finding a short non-zero $z$ with $Az = 0$).

**Fiat-Shamir with aborts** (Vadim Lyubashevsky's 2009 technique, the basis of Dilithium). Sign: pick a short random mask $y$, commit to the high bits $w_1$ of $Ay$, hash the commitment with the message to get a small challenge $c$, and respond $z = y + c s_1$. A verifier checks that $z$ is short and that $Az - ct$ matches the commitment. But $z$ is skewed in a direction related to $s_1$, so publishing every $z$ would leak the key over many signatures. The fix is **rejection sampling**: if any coefficient of $z$ (or of a second value involving $s_2$) is too big, the signer **throws the attempt away and starts over** with a new $y$. Published signatures then look independent of the key. FIPS 204 lists the expected number of attempts: 4.25 for ML-DSA-44, 5.1 for ML-DSA-65 and 3.85 for ML-DSA-87.

blocks.title: ML-DSA signing, simplified from FIPS 204 Algorithms 2 and 7
blocks.code:
def ml_dsa_sign(sk, msg, ctx=b""):
    m_prime = bytes([0, len(ctx)]) + ctx + msg   # domain separation
    mu = H(tr + m_prime)                          # tr = H(public key)
    rnd = random_bytes(32)                        # hedged; zeros if deterministic
    seed = H(K + rnd + mu)                        # K is secret, from sk
    kappa = 0
    while True:
        y = expand_mask(seed, kappa)              # short random mask
        w = A @ y
        w1 = high_bits(w)                         # the commitment
        c = sample_in_ball(c_tilde := H(mu + encode(w1)))  # few +-1s
        z = y + c * s1                            # the response
        if too_big(z) or too_big(low_bits(w - c * s2)):
            kappa += L                            # would leak s1 or s2:
            continue                              # abort and try again
        h = make_hint(...)                        # lets verifier rebuild w1
        return encode(c_tilde, z, h)

scenes.caption: The message is prefixed with 0, the context length and the context string, then hashed with tr, a hash of the public key. Binding the public key is part of ML-DSA's design.
Hedged signing (the default): fresh randomness rnd plus the secret K from the private key make the per-message seed. A broken RNG alone does not expose the key.
Attempt 1: derive the mask y, compute the commitment w1, hash it into the challenge c and form z = y + c s1 (c times s1).
z has a coefficient outside the allowed range, so publishing it could leak s1. Abort: advance kappa and loop. Nothing from this attempt leaves the signer.
Attempts 2 and 3 in this illustration: new masks, new challenges. The number of tries here is made up; on average ML-DSA-65 needs 5.1.

vars.result: z and low bits in range

scenes.caption: Success: compute the hint h that lets the verifier rebuild w1 from the compressed public key, and output the signature (3309 bytes for ML-DSA-65).

blocks.md:
**Options you will see in APIs.**

- **Hedged vs deterministic.** The default mixes fresh randomness into each signature. The deterministic variant sets rnd to 32 zero bytes; FIPS 204 allows it but warns it makes fault and side-channel attacks harder to mitigate. Compare crypto-building-blocks: ECDSA collapses if its per-message secret repeats (the PS3 case). ML-DSA also derives its seed from the secret $K$, so a weak RNG alone does not leak the key.
- **Context string.** Up to 255 bytes, signed along with the message. Using a different context per purpose (firmware, login, documents) stops a signature for one use from being accepted for another.
- **Pure vs HashML-DSA.** Pure ML-DSA signs the message itself and is the usual choice. HashML-DSA signs a pre-computed digest with a domain-separated encoding, for cases such as huge files; IR 8547 says the digest must be at least as strong as the parameter set.

blocks.code:
# Signer: generate an ML-DSA-65 key once and keep sk.pem in an HSM or vault
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out sk.pem
openssl pkey -in sk.pem -pubout -out pk.pem
printf 'firmware 1.4.2' > fw.bin

# Sign with a context string that names the purpose (domain separation)
openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin -inkey sk.pem -in fw.bin -out fw.sig \
  -pkeyopt context-string:fw-update-v1
wc -c < fw.sig

# Verifier: same key, same context: accepted
openssl pkeyutl -verify -rawin -pubin -inkey pk.pem -in fw.bin \
  -sigfile fw.sig -pkeyopt context-string:fw-update-v1

# Same signature presented for a different purpose: rejected
openssl pkeyutl -verify -rawin -pubin -inkey pk.pem -in fw.bin \
  -sigfile fw.sig -pkeyopt context-string:login-v1 2>/dev/null

# Output:
#     3309
# Signature Verified Successfully
# Signature Verification Failure
blocks.caption: ML-DSA-65 with a context string, using the OpenSSL 4.1 command line (real output; the error detail line is hidden). The same signature fails when verified under a different context.

blocks.title: Signature and public-key sizes (bytes)

scenes.caption: Signature sizes measured with OpenSSL 4.1: 64, 71 (DER-encoded, varies by a byte or two), 256, then 2420, 3309 and 4627 for ML-DSA.
Public keys (raw): 32, 65, 256 (the modulus), then 1312, 1952 and 2592. ML-DSA private keys are 2560 to 4896 bytes in full form, or a 32-byte seed.

blocks.question: Why does ML-DSA signing sometimes throw away its work and start over?
options: The random number generator failed
A candidate response z (or a related value) is too large, and publishing it would leak information about the secret vectors; rejection keeps signatures independent of the key
The message was too long
The context string was invalid
blocks.explain: This is the 'aborts' in Fiat-Shamir with aborts. Only responses inside a safe range are released; FIPS 204 lists the expected number of attempts per parameter set.

blocks.question: A firmware signature made with context 'fw-update-v1' is replayed to a login service that verifies with context 'login-v1' and the same public key. What happens?
options: It fails, because the context is part of what was signed
It verifies, because the key and message match
It verifies only for ML-DSA-87
It fails only if the signer used deterministic mode
blocks.explain: The signed message is 0 || len(ctx) || ctx || M, so a different context gives a different message. The OpenSSL run above shows exactly this failure.

lessons.title: SLH-DSA, LMS and XMSS: signatures from hash functions alone

blocks.md: Hash-based signatures need no new math at all: if the hash function is secure, so are they. That makes them the most conservative post-quantum choice, at the price of size or bookkeeping. The building block is a **hash chain**: take a secret $x$, hash it 15 times, and publish the end $H^{15}(x)$. To sign a digit $d$ from 0 to 15, reveal $H^{d}(x)$; the verifier hashes $15 - d$ more times and checks that the result is the published end.

One problem: anyone can hash **forward**, so from a signature on 5 a forger can produce one on 6. The fix is a **checksum** chain signed alongside: it signs $15 - d$, so raising the digit lowers the checksum, which would require hashing backward, and that is infeasible. NIST SP 800-208 explains the checksum this way. WOTS+ (Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus) in FIPS 205 does this for a whole digest: $2n + 3$ chains of 16 positions (15 hash steps), 35 chains when $n$ = 16 bytes.

blocks.code:
# TOY Winternitz-style one-time signature over ONE base-16 digit plus its
# checksum, to show hash chains. Real WOTS+ (FIPS 205) signs 2n+3 digits
# with keyed, address-separated hashes. Never use this outside a lesson.
import hashlib, os
W = 16                                   # chain length (digits 0..15)

def H(x, times):                         # walk 'times' steps down a hash chain
    for _ in range(times):
        x = hashlib.sha256(x).digest()[:16]
    return x

sk = [os.urandom(16), os.urandom(16)]    # chain starts: digit chain, checksum chain
pk = [H(s, W - 1) for s in sk]           # chain ends are public

def sign(digit):
    checksum = (W - 1) - digit           # raising the digit lowers the checksum
    return [H(sk[0], digit), H(sk[1], checksum)]

def verify(digit, sig):
    checksum = (W - 1) - digit
    return [H(sig[0], W - 1 - digit), H(sig[1], W - 1 - checksum)] == pk

sig = sign(5)
print("sign digit 5: reveal step 5 of chain A and step 10 of chain B")
print("verify(5): ", verify(5, sig))
print("verify(6): ", verify(6, sig))    # same signature, different digit

# Output:
# sign digit 5: reveal step 5 of chain A and step 10 of chain B
# verify(5):  True
# verify(6):  False
blocks.caption: A toy one-digit Winternitz signature in Python 3 (real output). The checksum chain is what stops the forgery: a signature on 5 does not verify as a signature on 6.

blocks.md: **From one-time to many-time: Merkle trees.** Put many one-time public keys at the leaves of a binary hash tree (a Merkle tree) and publish only the root. A signature is a one-time signature plus the **authentication path**: the sibling hashes needed to recompute the root. **XMSS** (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) and **LMS** (Leighton-Micali Signatures) work this way and are standardised in NIST SP 800-208 (2020). Their catch is **state**: the signer must remember which leaves are used, because signing two different messages with the same one-time key lets an attacker forge signatures.

blocks.title: A Merkle tree of four one-time keys

scenes.caption: Four one-time public keys L0 to L3 at the leaves; pairs are hashed up to a single root. The root (with a public seed) is the whole public key: 32 bytes for SLH-DSA level 1.
Sign a message with one-time key L2. The signature carries the WOTS+ signature and identifies leaf 2.
Authentication path: the verifier receives L3 and H(L0 || L1), rebuilds H(L2 || L3) and then the root, and compares it with the public key.
Stateful schemes (LMS, XMSS): the signer must record that leaf 2 is spent before releasing the signature. Next time it must use leaf 3.
SLH-DSA removes the state: a tree of trees (hypertree) certifies 2^63 to 2^68 few-time FORS keys, and the message hash picks one pseudorandomly.

blocks.md: **SLH-DSA** (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 205, from SPHINCS+) avoids state with sheer size. Its key pair conceptually holds $2^{63}$ to $2^{68}$ keys for **FORS** (Forest of Random Subsets, a few-time scheme), certified by a hypertree of XMSS trees. Each signature uses a FORS key chosen pseudorandomly from the message hash; occasional reuse is safe because FORS tolerates a few signatures per key. Parameter sets allow $2^{64}$ signatures per key pair, which FIPS 205 notes would take over 58 years at 10 billion signatures per second. The "s" sets are small but slow to sign; the "f" sets are fast but larger.

blocks.title: Signature size and speed (OpenSSL 4.1, Apple M5 Pro, one core)

scenes.caption: Signature bytes: 64, 3309, 7856 and 17088. The two SLH-DSA sets trade size for speed. Public keys: 32, 1952, 32 and 32 bytes.
Signatures per second measured with openssl speed: about 65,700, 3,190, 17 and 350. SLH-DSA-128s needs about 60 ms per signature on this machine.
Verifications per second: about 26,500, 16,600, 16,900 and 5,900. Verifying is cheap for all of them, which suits keys that sign rarely and are checked often.

blocks.md: **Stateful keys in practice.** SP 800-208 requires LMS and XMSS keys to be generated and used in hardware cryptographic modules that never export private keys, even encrypted, and it requires the state to be updated in non-volatile memory **before** a signature is released. It warns that an ordinary file write may sit in a cache and be lost on a crash, and recommends monotonic counters where available. Restoring a key from backup or cloning a signing machine rolls the counter back, which is exactly how reuse happens. NIST and IR 8547 therefore aim stateful schemes at narrow uses such as firmware signing.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, os

STATE = "lms_state.txt"                       # index of the next unused one-time key

def ots_sign(leaf, msg):                      # stand-in for a real LMS/XMSS signer
    return hashlib.sha256(b"%d|" % leaf + msg).hexdigest()[:16]

def read_index():
    return int(open(STATE).read()) if os.path.exists(STATE) else 0

def sign_unsafe(msg):
    leaf = read_index()
    sig = ots_sign(leaf, msg)                 # signature can leave the box...
    open(STATE, "w").write(str(leaf + 1))     # ...before the new index is durable
    return leaf, sig                          # crash here: leaf is used again later

def sign_safe(msg):
    leaf = read_index()
    tmp = STATE + ".tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w") as f:                 # 1. reserve the leaf first
        f.write(str(leaf + 1)); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
    os.replace(tmp, STATE)                    # atomic rename
    dfd = os.open(".", os.O_RDONLY); os.fsync(dfd); os.close(dfd)
    return leaf, ots_sign(leaf, msg)          # 2. only now sign and release

print(sign_safe(b"firmware 1.4.2"), sign_safe(b"firmware 1.4.3"))

# Output:
# (0, 'cf22c26560add01e') (1, 'cd3a1769e27fdd73')
blocks.caption: Vulnerable and fixed ordering for a stateful signer (Python 3, real output; ots_sign is a stand-in). The fix reserves the leaf durably, with fsync and an atomic rename, before any signature exists.

blocks.md: Choosing: **ML-DSA** is NIST's general-purpose default. **SLH-DSA** suits long-lived roots of trust where you want the fewest assumptions and can afford big, slow signatures. **LMS/XMSS** suit firmware signing done in an HSM with strict state control. **FN-DSA** (from Falcon, still being standardised) has the smallest lattice signatures, but Cloudflare warns that safe signing needs constant-time floating-point arithmetic, which has proved hard to implement.

blocks.question: Your firmware signer uses LMS on a virtual machine that operations staff restore from last night's snapshot after a crash. What is the risk?
options: None: LMS is stateless
The public key changes
Signatures become larger
The restored state points at one-time keys that were already used, so the next signatures reuse them and an attacker who sees both can forge signatures
blocks.explain: Rolling back state is the classic way stateful hash-based keys get reused. SP 800-208 requires signing in a hardware module that does not export keys; or use stateless SLH-DSA where that is impractical.

blocks.question: Why does SLH-DSA not need to track state?
options: It uses each one-time key exactly once by keeping a counter in the public key
Each signature uses a few-time FORS key picked pseudorandomly from an enormous set, and FORS stays secure even if a key is occasionally picked twice
It is a lattice scheme
It refuses to sign the same message twice
blocks.explain: With 2^63 to 2^68 FORS keys and few-time security, random selection makes harmful reuse negligible for up to 2^64 signatures. The cost is signature size: 7856 bytes even for the small level-1 set.

lessons.title: Hybrid designs: combiners, Signal, iMessage and SSH

blocks.md:
tls-pki showed the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768: both shares travel in one key_share, and the two 32-byte secrets are concatenated into HKDF-Extract. A hybrid aims to stay secure if **either** component is unbroken (RFC 9954). Whether it achieves that depends on the **combiner**, the function that merges the secrets.

**Why plain concatenation is fine inside TLS 1.3.** RFC 9954 relies on two facts: every share and secret has a **fixed length** once the group is negotiated, so the concatenation is unambiguous, and the TLS key schedule mixes the secrets with a hash of the whole handshake **transcript**, which includes both public shares and ciphertexts. Under those conditions the construction matches a combiner proven secure. RFC 10024 adds a warning: the analysis "relies crucially on the TLS 1.3 message transcript, and one cannot assume a similar hybridization is secure in other protocols."

**Outside TLS, include more than the secrets.** NIST SP 800-227 shows that the simple combiner $K = \mathrm{KDF}(K_1, K_2)$ does not, in general, keep the IND-CCA security of the stronger component, whatever KDF you use. It recommends hashing the ciphertexts and encapsulation keys as well, with a **domain separator** that names the exact construction. IR 8547 lets a FIPS-validated system use a hybrid as long as one input comes from an approved scheme: SP 800-56C allows the shared secret $Z' = Z \,\|\, T$ when $Z$ comes from an approved scheme, and NIST plans to let $Z$ come from ML-KEM and to allow either order. That is why RFC 10024 puts the ML-KEM secret **first** in X25519MLKEM768 (ML-KEM is the approved part) but the ECDH secret first in SecP256r1MLKEM768, whose P-256 half is approved.

blocks.caption: The IND-CCA-preserving shape SP 800-227 describes: both secrets, both ciphertexts, both encapsulation keys and a label naming the scheme, all fixed-length.
A hybrid KEM for your own protocol in Go 1.24 (real output). Errors are ignored only to keep the listing short; production code must check every one.

blocks.md: **Case: Signal's PQXDH (September 2023).** Signal's asynchronous handshake, X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman), lets Alice start a chat while Bob is offline, using keys Bob uploaded earlier. [PQXDH](https://signal.org/docs/specifications/pqxdh/) (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman) adds a signed post-quantum prekey: Alice encapsulates to it with CRYSTALS-Kyber-1024 and mixes the result into the session key, $SK = \mathrm{KDF}(DH_1 \| DH_2 \| DH_3 \| DH_4 \| SS)$. The specification says this defends against harvest-now-decrypt-later, while mutual authentication still relies on the discrete-log problem in that revision. When Bob's one-time KEM prekeys run out, Alice uses a **last-resort** prekey that can serve many sessions, one reason the KEM must be IND-CCA secure (lesson 7).

blocks.title: PQXDH: starting a post-quantum chat with someone offline

scenes.caption: Bob uploads an identity key, a signed curve prekey, signed Kyber prekeys (one-time ones plus a last-resort one) and one-time curve prekeys.
Alice fetches a prekey bundle and verifies Bob's signatures on the prekeys. If any check fails, Alice aborts.
Alice computes up to four X25519 results and one Kyber encapsulation, and derives SK = KDF(DH1 || DH2 || DH3 || DH4 || SS).
Alice's first message carries Alice's identity and ephemeral keys, the Kyber ciphertext, prekey identifiers and the first AEAD-encrypted message.
Bob repeats the DH computations, decapsulates the ciphertext and gets the same SK. A recorded session now needs both X25519 and Kyber broken.

blocks.md: **What came next.** Signal's [Sparse Post Quantum Ratchet](https://signal.org/blog/spqr/) (SPQR, October 2025) keeps adding fresh ML-KEM secrets during a conversation, not only at the start, mixing them with the existing Double Ratchet (Signal's per-message key update) into a "Triple Ratchet". Because ML-KEM-768 keys and ciphertexts are over 1000 bytes each against 32 for ECDH, it splits them across messages with erasure codes, which let the receiver rebuild a key from enough of the chunks. Apple's [iMessage PQ3](https://security.apple.com/blog/imessage-pq3/) (February 2024, iOS 17.4) registers a Kyber-1024 key next to a P-256 ECDH key per device, signs both with an ECDSA key held in the Secure Enclave (Apple's on-chip key store), and rekeys with post-quantum material periodically rather than on every message. Douglas Stebila of the University of Waterloo analysed PQ3 and found its keys secure as long as either the ECDH problem or Kyber holds.

**SSH got there first.** OpenSSH has used a post-quantum hybrid by default since [version 9.0](https://www.openssh.com/pq.html) (April 2022), initially sntrup761x25519-sha512, which pairs X25519 with the lattice-based KEM sntrup761. Version 9.9 added mlkem768x25519-sha256, which became the default in 10.0 (April 2025), and 10.1 warns when a connection uses a non-post-quantum key exchange.

blocks.code:
ssh -V
ssh -Q kex | grep -E 'mlkem|sntrup'

# Output:
# OpenSSH_10.3p1, LibreSSL 3.3.6
# sntrup761x25519-sha512
# sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com
# mlkem768x25519-sha256
blocks.caption: Checking which post-quantum key exchanges your SSH client supports (real output on a macOS test machine). Run ssh -Q kex on servers too, or use ssh -v to see what a connection negotiated.

blocks.md: Hybrid means "secure if either part holds", but only with a sound combiner. Inside TLS 1.3 and SSH, the protocol transcript makes simple concatenation safe. In your own protocol, hash both secrets together with both ciphertexts, both public keys and a label, and keep every input fixed-length.

blocks.question: You design a file-encryption format that combines X25519 and ML-KEM-768. Which key derivation is the safest choice?
options: K = K1 XOR K2
K = SHA-256(K1 || K2), because concatenation is what TLS does
K = SHA3-256(K1 || K2 || c1 || c2 || ek1 || ek2 || label naming the format and version)
K = K1 alone, with K2 sent as a backup
blocks.explain: TLS 1.3's concatenation is safe because of its transcript hashing. A standalone format has no transcript, and SP 800-227 shows KDF(K1, K2) alone does not generically preserve IND-CCA security; binding ciphertexts, keys and a domain label does.

blocks.question: PQXDH protects a chat recorded today against a future quantum computer. What does its 2023 revision NOT yet protect against?
options: An attacker with a quantum computer at the time of the handshake impersonating a party, because authentication still relies on discrete logs
Passive recording of the initial handshake
Loss of Bob's one-time prekeys
Message reordering
blocks.explain: The specification states that PQXDH gives post-quantum forward secrecy but still relies on the discrete-log problem for mutual authentication. An active attacker needs a quantum computer during the handshake, not years later.

lessons.title: Rolling it out: browsers, middleboxes and big certificates

blocks.md: **The road to default-on (from Cloudflare's 2025 timeline and Chrome's announcements).** Google's first post-quantum experiment in Chrome ran in July 2016, the year NIST's competition began, followed by a joint Cloudflare and Google experiment in June 2018. Cloudflare enabled post-quantum key agreement on its servers by default in October 2022. Chrome 116 (August 2023) added X25519Kyber768, ramped to 10% of desktop users in November 2023 and enabled it by default on desktop in March 2024. Go enabled it by default in August 2024. In November 2024 Chrome switched to the standard X25519MLKEM768 (Chrome 131), enabled it on Android, and Firefox enabled it on desktop. OpenSSL made it default in April 2025, and Apple's iOS, iPadOS and macOS 26 from autumn 2025.

Chrome's switch is a lesson in identifiers: the final ML-KEM is incompatible with the Kyber draft, so the TLS code point changed from 0x6399 to 0x11EC, and Chrome [chose not to offer both](https://security.googleblog.com/2024/09/a-new-path-for-kyber-on-web.html) because two post-quantum key shares in one ClientHello would be too big. Servers had to support both during the change-over to keep every client post-quantum.

blocks.title: Post-quantum key agreement seen by Cloudflare (percent)

scenes.caption: Browser-side adoption: nearly 2% of TLS 1.3 connections to Cloudflare in March 2024; by the last week of October 2025 the majority of human-initiated traffic (drawn as 50, a lower bound).
Origin servers behind Cloudflare lag far behind: 0.5% supported post-quantum key agreement in 2023 and 3.7% in 2025. Clients update automatically; servers need someone to act.

blocks.md: **Why it took years: ossification.** Protocol ossification means software in the path hard-codes assumptions about what traffic looks like, so the protocol can no longer change. A hybrid ClientHello is over a kilobyte larger and no longer fits in one packet. The [tldr.fail](https://tldr.fail/) project documents servers that call TCP read() once, get only part of the ClientHello, and reject the connection instead of reading the rest or ignoring the unknown group. Cloudflare's review says that without these compatibility problems Chrome would likely have ramped up post-quantum key agreement about five years earlier.

blocks.title: The split ClientHello bug

scenes.caption: A hybrid ClientHello (over 1200 bytes of key share alone) is split by TCP into two segments.
The buggy server parses whatever its first read() returned, sees a truncated message and aborts. The client never gets a fallback.
A correct server keeps reading until the whole record arrives. Without post-quantum support it simply picks a classical group it knows; with support it picks the hybrid.

blocks.md: **The second migration: certificates.** Key agreement was the easy part. Cloudflare counts **five signatures and two public keys** in a first visit: the root's signature on the intermediate certificate, the intermediate's public key and its signature on the leaf, the leaf's public key and its signature on the handshake, and two SCT signatures for certificate transparency (from tls-pki). With ML-DSA-44 that is $5 \times 2420 + 2 \times 1312 = 14{,}724$ bytes, Cloudflare's "15 kB", against about 450 bytes for ECDSA P-256. RFC 9881 (October 2025) already defines how ML-DSA goes into X.509 certificates.

blocks.title: Authentication bytes in a first TLS visit (5 sigs, 2 public keys)

scenes.caption: Raw sizes, simplified (encodings add a little): ECDSA 5 x 64 + 2 x 65 = 450; RSA-2048 5 x 256 + 2 x 256 = 1792.
ML-DSA-44: 14,724 bytes; ML-DSA-65: 5 x 3309 + 2 x 1952 = 20,449 bytes. That is why Chrome wants to solve certificate size before deploying post-quantum certificates.

blocks.code:
# Same subject, three key types: compare certificate sizes (DER bytes)
for alg in EC:P-256 ML-DSA-44 ML-DSA-65; do
  case $alg in EC:*) opt="-newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:${alg#EC:}";;
               *)    opt="-newkey $alg";; esac
  openssl req -x509 $opt -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem \
      -subj "/CN=api.example.internal" -days 90 2>/dev/null
  printf '%-10s %5s bytes  ' "$alg" "$(openssl x509 -in c.pem -outform DER | wc -c | tr -d ' ')"
  openssl x509 -in c.pem -noout -text | grep -m1 "Signature Algorithm" | sed 's/^ *//'
done

# Output:
# EC:P-256     374 bytes  Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256
# ML-DSA-44   3970 bytes  Signature Algorithm: ML-DSA-44
# ML-DSA-65   5499 bytes  Signature Algorithm: ML-DSA-65
blocks.caption: Real certificate sizes from OpenSSL 4.1 for the same subject. One ML-DSA-44 certificate is more than ten times an ECDSA one, and a chain has two or three.

blocks.md: Cloudflare estimates that adding ML-DSA to its roughly 18 million TLS connections per second would take 2.1 Tbps, about 0.5% of its network capacity: affordable in bandwidth, though Cloudflare's open question is what the extra bytes do to handshake performance. The leading fix is **Merkle Tree Certificates**, a proposal in which, in the common case, every signature except the handshake signature is replaced by a Merkle-tree proof of under 800 bytes; Cloudflare and Chrome planned to trial it. In a lab you can already run a fully post-quantum handshake: OpenSSL 4.1 negotiated the pure ML-KEM group and an ML-DSA-65 certificate between a local s_server and s_client, reporting "Signature type: mldsa65" and "Negotiated TLS1.3 group: MLKEM768".

Defender view. **Prevent**: enable X25519MLKEM768 on load balancers, CDNs and origins (the laggards), and test every TLS-terminating box with a ClientHello split across packets. **Detect**: log the negotiated group per connection and track the post-quantum share; alert on failures seen only with large ClientHellos. **Respond**: Chrome's PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled policy can switch it off temporarily, but the fix is the broken middlebox.

blocks.question: Why did browsers take years to turn on post-quantum key agreement by default?
options: ML-KEM was too slow for browsers
Some middleboxes and servers assumed the ClientHello fits in one packet and failed on the larger hybrid one instead of falling back
Certificate authorities refused to issue ML-KEM certificates
TLS 1.3 had no way to negotiate new groups
blocks.explain: TLS already negotiates groups cleanly; buggy implementations broke that. Cloudflare estimates Chrome would have ramped up about five years earlier without these compatibility issues. ML-KEM is actually fast.

blocks.question: Roughly how many extra bytes would ML-DSA-44 add to the authentication part of a first TLS visit (5 signatures, 2 public keys), compared with ECDSA P-256?
