options: About 1.5 kB
None: signature sizes are similar
About 150 kB
About 15 kB
blocks.explain: 5 x 2420 + 2 x 1312 = 14,724 bytes versus about 450, so roughly 14 kB more. This is the 'second migration' problem that Merkle Tree Certificates aim to solve.

lessons.title: Crypto inventory and agility: finding every RSA before 2030

blocks.md: You cannot migrate what you cannot find. IR 8547 tells organisations to begin with **cryptographic inventories**, migration planning and early deployments. Public-key cryptography hides in more places than TLS: SSH, VPNs (IKE, Internet Key Exchange, and IPsec), code and firmware signing, S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) and PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) email, document signing, smart cards and PIV credentials (the US government's Personal Identity Verification cards), databases that wrap keys with RSA, HSMs and TPMs (Trusted Platform Modules), vendor appliances and libraries compiled into products you do not control.

blocks.title: From discovery to a migration backlog

nodes.label:
Certificates, CT logs,
HSM and KMS keys

Rank: data lifetime X,
exposure, upgradability

scenes.caption: Four discovery sources. Each finds what the others miss: scans see only what answers on the network, code scans miss vendor boxes, and nobody scans a smart card.
Everything lands in one inventory, ideally in a standard format such as a CycloneDX CBOM (Cryptography Bill of Materials): algorithm, key size, where, who owns it.
Rank each item: how long the data it protects must stay secret (Mosca's X), whether recorded traffic is exposed (key exchange), and whether the thing can be updated at all.
The output is an ordered backlog: HNDL-exposed key exchange first, then long-lived signatures and devices that cannot be patched, then everything else before 2035.

blocks.md: **Network discovery you can run today.** For TLS, record the key-exchange group each endpoint negotiates (not just the protocol version) and the signature algorithm of its certificate. For SSH, list the key exchanges each server offers. NIST's NCCoE (National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence) is writing practice guides for this discovery step, and [CycloneDX CBOM](https://cyclonedx.org/capabilities/cbom/) gives a standard format for the results. Scan only systems you own or are authorised to test.

blocks.code:
# Inventory: record the key exchange each endpoint negotiates. Two public
# sites are a demo; in practice list only hosts you own or may test.
for hp in www.cloudflare.com:443 example.com:443 localhost:8443; do
  out=$(echo | openssl s_client -connect "$hp" -servername "${hp%:*}" \
        -brief 2>&1)
  kx=$(echo "$out" | sed -n -e 's/^Negotiated TLS1.3 group: //p' \
                            -e 's/^Peer Temp Key: \([^,]*\).*/\1/p')
  case "$kx" in
    *[0-9]MLKEM*) verdict="PQ hybrid" ;;
    MLKEM*)  verdict="PQ only" ;;
    "")      verdict="no TLS 1.3 / unreachable" ;;
    *)       verdict="CLASSICAL: harvest-now risk" ;;
  esac
  printf '%-22s %-16s %s\n' "$hp" "$kx" "$verdict"
done

# Output:
# www.cloudflare.com:443 X25519MLKEM768   PQ hybrid
# example.com:443        X25519MLKEM768   PQ hybrid
# localhost:8443         X25519           CLASSICAL: harvest-now risk
blocks.caption: A minimal TLS inventory probe with the OpenSSL 4.1 client (real output). localhost:8443 is a test server limited to X25519, standing in for an internal service that has not been upgraded.

blocks.md:
**Crypto agility** is, in the words of NIST's 2025 white paper [CSWP 39](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/cswp/39/considerations-for-achieving-cryptographic-agility/final), "the capabilities needed to replace and adapt cryptographic algorithms in protocols, applications, software, hardware, firmware, and infrastructures while preserving security and ongoing operations." In code that means:

- **Algorithm identifiers travel with data**: every stored ciphertext, signature and key says which algorithm made it, so old data stays readable after the default changes.
- **One place decides**: callers ask a registry or crypto service for "the current KEM", never call RSA directly.
- **Policy is configuration**: allowed and preferred algorithms come from config, so retiring one is a deploy, not a rewrite.
- **Headroom**: database columns, protocol length fields, packet sizes and HSM slots sized for multi-kilobyte keys and signatures.

blocks.caption: A small KEM registry in Go 1.24 (real output). Callers name an algorithm ID; the policy table refuses X25519-only for new data once the organisation requires post-quantum protection.

blocks.md: Agility has a price you met in tls-pki: anything that negotiates can be **downgraded**. Keep the allowed list short, remove algorithms rather than leaving them enabled "just in case", and authenticate the negotiation (as TLS 1.3 does by signing the transcript). An unauthenticated algorithm field is an attacker's choice, not yours.

blocks.question: Your scan shows the public website negotiates X25519MLKEM768, but an internal API used by mobile apps still negotiates plain X25519. What should the inventory record and why?
options: The API as classical key exchange with the data it carries and how long that data must stay secret, because recorded traffic to it can be decrypted after Q-day
Nothing: internal APIs are not exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later
Only the API's certificate algorithm
Mark it compliant because the public site is post-quantum
blocks.explain: HNDL applies to any recorded traffic, internal or not, and mobile traffic crosses networks you do not control. The inventory needs the algorithm and the data lifetime to rank it.

blocks.question: Which design best supports crypto agility for stored encrypted files?
options: Hard-code ML-KEM-768 everywhere so nobody can choose a weak algorithm
Let each client choose any algorithm it likes
Store an algorithm identifier with each file and route all encryption through one registry driven by a policy file
Re-encrypt every file whenever the policy changes
blocks.explain: Identifiers keep old files readable, the registry keeps the code in one place, and a policy file makes retirement a configuration change. Free client choice invites downgrades; hard-coding just recreates the RSA problem with a new name.

lessons.title: Deadlines and a migration plan you can defend

blocks.md: **NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026).** NIST will **deprecate** all quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and **disallow** them under its standards after 2035, at every strength: ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA signatures; finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and MQV (Menezes-Qu-Vanstone) key agreement; and RSA key establishment. *Deprecated* means it may still be used if the data owner accepts the risk; *disallowed* means it may no longer be used for that purpose; *legacy use* means only processing already-protected data, such as decrypting old files or verifying old signatures. NIST's earlier plan had disallowed 112-bit public-key schemes on 1 January 2031; the quantum transition replaced it with this single schedule.

**US federal systems.** IR 8547 cites Executive Order 14412 and OMB (Office of Management and Budget) Memorandum M-26-15: mitigate as much quantum risk as feasible by 31 December 2030; high value assets and high impact systems must use post-quantum key establishment by **31 December 2030** and post-quantum signatures by **31 December 2031**; agencies must support TLS 1.3 by 2 January 2030. National Security Memorandum 10 (May 2022) set 2035 as the target for completing the federal migration, which still stands. National security systems follow the US National Security Agency's stricter CNSA 2.0 (below).

**Europe and the UK.** The EU's coordinated roadmap (June 2025) asks member states to start national transitions by the end of 2026, finish high-risk use cases by the end of 2030 and medium-risk ones by the end of 2035. The UK National Cyber Security Centre's (NCSC) [timeline](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/pqc-migration-timelines) is: discovery and an initial plan by 2028, highest-priority migrations by 2031, everything by 2035.

blocks.title: Key PQC deadlines (years from 1 January 2026)

scenes.caption: NIST: classical public-key crypto acceptable to the end of 2030, deprecated 2031 to 2035, disallowed from 2036. The marker is now, late 2026.
US federal high value assets (HVA): post-quantum key establishment by the end of 2030 and signatures by the end of 2031; everything by 2035 (NSM-10).
EU and UK: plans now (EU by end 2026, UK discovery by 2028), high-risk or priority systems by 2030 to 2031, the rest by 2035. Every regime converges on 2035.

blocks.md:
**What NIST says to migrate to (IR 8547).** Key establishment: ML-KEM, with ML-KEM-768 the recommended default; HQC will join once its standard is published. Signatures: ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87, SLH-DSA, and the stateful LMS/HSS and XMSS for narrow uses; a standard derived from Falcon is in development. Symmetric cryptography at 128 bits or more stays. Hybrids are welcome and FIPS 140 (the US standard for validating cryptographic modules) can validate them when one component is approved, but IR 8547 expects them to be **temporary**, followed by a second transition to post-quantum-only algorithms. That second transition is why agility matters.

**National security systems: CNSA 2.0.** The NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 (September 2022) is stricter: only ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 (category 5), LMS or XMSS for software and firmware signing, AES-256, and SHA-384 or SHA-512. Exclusive use is required by 2030 for code and firmware signing and network equipment (VPNs, routers), and by 2033 for browsers, servers, cloud services and operating systems.

**A plan you can defend**, assembled from IR 8547, the NCSC and the EU roadmap:

1. **Own it.** Name an owner and budget; the migration spans years and teams.
2. **Inventory** (lesson 14), including suppliers and devices.
3. **Prioritise** with Mosca's inequality: long-lived secrets over recorded channels first, then signatures on things that cannot be updated.
4. **Take the free wins**: hybrid key exchange is already the default in current browsers, OpenSSL, Go, Apple's OSes and OpenSSH. Upgrade servers, load balancers and origins so it is actually negotiated.
5. **Buy post-quantum**: require PQC support in procurement; IR 8547 and OMB tell agencies to identify systems that cannot support it for replacement or decommissioning.
6. **Plan signatures and PKI**: HSM support, ML-DSA certificate profiles (RFC 9881), firmware signing with ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or LMS.
7. **Test** for ClientHello and certificate size, latency and middlebox failures before each rollout.
8. **Stay agile** for the hybrid-to-pure step and for whatever cryptanalysis brings next.

Dates differ by regulator, but the order of work does not: inventory, then key establishment on anything recorded today, then signatures, PKI and devices, all finished by 2035. The NIST dates apply at every key size; a 4096-bit RSA key is deprecated after 2030 like a 2048-bit one.

**Practise legally.** Use only systems you own or are authorised to test.

- Build the lab from this course on your own machine: OpenSSL 3.5 or later for ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA keys, a local s_server and s_client pair with hybrid and pure post-quantum groups, and Go's crypto/mlkem.
- [Open Quantum Safe](https://openquantumsafe.org/): open-source liboqs and integrations for experimenting with post-quantum algorithms in protocols.
- [CryptoHack](https://cryptohack.org/): a free platform of interactive puzzles for learning modern cryptography.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF): free security exercises and competitions.
- Inventory your own estate: run the TLS and SSH probes from lesson 14 against hosts you administer and record the results as a CBOM.

blocks.question: Under IR 8547, an ECDSA P-384 signing key is still in use in 2032. What is its status?
options: Disallowed: all classical signatures were disallowed after 2030
Deprecated: still usable if the data owner accepts the risk, and disallowed after 2035 under NIST standards
Acceptable, because P-384 gives 192-bit classical security
Legacy use only: it can verify but not sign
blocks.explain: IR 8547 deprecates quantum-vulnerable signatures after 2030 regardless of strength and disallows them after 2035. Federal high value assets face the earlier OMB deadlines on top of that.

blocks.question: A US agency runs a high-impact system. By when must it use post-quantum key establishment under the policy IR 8547 cites?
options: 2 January 2030
31 December 2035
31 December 2031
31 December 2030
blocks.explain: OMB M-26-15 requires post-quantum key establishment for high value assets and high impact systems by 31 December 2030 and signatures by 31 December 2031. 2 January 2030 is the TLS 1.3 support deadline; 2035 is the overall NSM-10 target.
